cheatsheet:
## Why other models exist (lesson 1)

Tables make three things hard: changing the shape of records (every row has the same columns), keeping data that's read together in one place (locality), and growing past one machine. Each family of stores gives up joins, transactions across many records, or a shape that the store checks, to make one of them cheap.

| | Schema-on-write | Schema-on-read |
|---|---|---|
| Who checks a record's shape | the store, on every write | every program that reads it |
| Example | a table; a `CHECK` on a `jsonb` column; a MongoDB 9.0 validator at the `constraint` level | a document store with no validator |
| Wins when | every record has the same shape | records really differ (a sign-up form per country, data from partners) |

## The families

| Family | You store | You find it by | In this track |
|---|---|---|---|
| Key-value | a value, or an item of named attributes, under a key | its key, or a sorted run of items under one partition key | DynamoDB (lessons 3, 4) |
| Wide-column (not a column store) | partitions of sorted rows, with columns per row | the partition key, then a slice of the clustering columns | Cassandra 5.0 (lesson 5) |
| Document | trees of fields, like JSON | any indexed field | MongoDB 9.0, PostgreSQL `jsonb` (lesson 6) |
| Property graph | nodes and relationships, both with properties | a start node, then a walk | SQL/PGQ (lesson 7), Neo4j 2026.10 (lesson 8) |
| Triples and rules | facts of subject, predicate, object; recursive rules | triple patterns; rules run until nothing new appears | RDF, SPARQL, Datalog (lesson 9) |

Search, time-series and vector stores are mostly one special index on top of these models. Bigtable (2006) keeps keys sorted and cuts them into ranges. Dynamo (2007) hashes keys onto a ring of machines and copies each key to N of them. DynamoDB shares Dynamo's name and its hashing, but each partition has one leader, which its copies elect with Multi-Paxos.

## Keys come from the questions (lessons 2 to 5)

- Write down every access pattern, a question the app asks, with how often it runs, before you choose a key.
- Partition key: give `=` on all its parts; it picks the partition, the group of items stored together. Sort key or clustering columns: sorted inside the partition; give `=` on the first parts, then one range, with no gaps.
- Every query is a key lookup, a range read or a scan (a read of everything). A filter runs after the read, and pays for everything read.
- A question the key can't answer needs another copy of the data: a global secondary index in DynamoDB (it lags a moment behind), another table in Cassandra, another index in MongoDB. Each copy costs a write.
- DynamoDB: a read unit covers 4 KB read strongly consistently, and a write unit covers 1 KB. Each partition tops out at 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second, and an item is at most 400 KB. Single-table design keeps everything one screen needs under one partition key.
- Cassandra partition: keep it under 100,000 rows and 100 MB. Rows = write rate x bucket length, so add a time bucket sized for the busiest key.

## Writes that can't race

| Need | DynamoDB | Cassandra | MongoDB | PostgreSQL `jsonb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Insert once | condition `attribute_not_exists(pk)` | `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS` (a Paxos round) | unique (partial) index | primary key, `ON CONFLICT` |
| Check and change one record | condition expression | `UPDATE ... IF` | `updateOne` with the check in its filter | `UPDATE ... WHERE` with the check |
| Several records together | `TransactWriteItems`: 100 actions, 4 MB, 2 writes per item | logged batch: all applied in the end, but readers can see it half done | multi-document transaction | any transaction |

Cassandra never deletes in place. A delete writes a tombstone, a marker kept for `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days). A read warns past 1,000 tombstones and fails past 100,000, so don't use a partition as a queue.

## Graphs (lessons 7 to 9)

- `WITH RECURSIVE`: the anchor runs once; the recursive term reads only the previous round's rows (the working table) until a round finds nothing. PostgreSQL has no depth limit and notices no cycles: add `CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path`.
- SQL/PGQ (SQL:2023): `CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH` over tables, `GRAPH_TABLE (g MATCH ... COLUMNS ...)`. It runs in Oracle 23ai and 26ai, Spanner Graph and DuckDB through `duckpgq`, not in PostgreSQL 18 or 19.
- Cypher 25: `(a:Account)-[:USES]->(x)`; repeats with `((...)-[...]->(...)){1,3}` and `-[:TRANSFERRED_TO]->{3,6}`. Start from a uniqueness constraint (`NodeUniqueIndexSeek`), put an upper bound on every walk, and keep supernodes out.
- GQL (ISO/IEC 39075:2024) made Cypher's pattern style a standard; Cypher 25 covers most of its required features.
- RDF stores triples with global names (IRIs). A SPARQL query is a join of triple patterns, and `ex:owns+` walks any depth. RDF 1.2 is a W3C Candidate Recommendation (April 2026).
- Datalog: `controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z).` Semi-naive evaluation joins only the last round's new facts, which is what PostgreSQL's working table does.
- GraphQL is a query language for APIs, over any store. One resolver per field makes 1 + N + N calls; a loader per level makes one call per level.

## Pairs people mix up

| | | The difference |
|---|---|---|
| Wide-column store | Column store | Wide-column (Cassandra): partitions of rows, each row with its own columns. Column store: each column kept together on disk, built for adding up (the Storage engines track). |
| Dynamo | DynamoDB | Dynamo, the 2007 paper: equal machines, no leader, writes that keep going through failures. DynamoDB, Amazon's service: one elected leader per partition. |
| Schemaless | No schema | Schemaless means schema-on-read: the shape is still there, in every reader's code. |
| GQL | GraphQL | GQL: the ISO standard language for graph databases. GraphQL: a query language for APIs, over any store. |
| `w: 1` | `w: "majority"` | `w: 1`: OK once the primary has the write, which a failover can lose. `w: "majority"`: OK once most members have it, so it survives (MongoDB's default since 5.0). |
| `UNION ALL` | `UNION` | In a recursive CTE, `UNION` drops exact repeats, so it stops a cycle only when each row holds the node id alone. |
recap: Tables make three things hard: changing the shape of records, keeping data that's read together in one place, and growing past one machine. Every other model gives up joins, transactions across many records or a checked shape to make one of them cheap.
Schemaless means schema-on-read: the shape moves into every reader's code. MongoDB 9.0's `constraint` level and PostgreSQL `jsonb` with CHECK constraints show the two worlds meeting.
Design keys from the questions: write every access pattern down first, make each one a key lookup or a range read, and remember that every extra copy (an index, another table) costs a write.

DynamoDB is a key-value store of sorted item collections, with limits per partition (3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second, items up to 400 KB). Single-table design stores a screen's records under one key, and `TransactWriteItems` makes up to 100 writes happen together or not at all.
Cassandra's wide-column model is partitions of sorted rows, not a column store. Size partitions with time buckets, and remember that every delete leaves a tombstone for 10 days.

A document keeps what's read and changed together in one record that changes in one step. A PostgreSQL `jsonb` column gives the same model next to joins and transactions. MongoDB adds indexes inside documents and sharding, and only `w: "majority"` writes survive a failover.

Questions of unknown depth need a loop: WITH RECURSIVE (with CYCLE) in SQL, SQL/PGQ in Oracle, Spanner and DuckDB, or Cypher 25 in Neo4j, whose pattern style GQL made a standard. Start every walk from an index, and bound it.
RDF triples and SPARQL turn a question into a join of patterns, Datalog's recursive rules run semi-naively to a fixpoint, and GraphQL is a language for APIs whose N+1 resolver calls need batching.

The limit across the track: every model makes some questions cheap by making others dear, and the choice is made when you pick the key. How each store keeps its records on disk is the next track, Storage engines and query execution.

quiz.q: A team wants to move shop sign-up forms, which differ by country and change every quarter, off a table with 140 mostly empty (NULL) columns. Which statement about a document store is accurate?
options: It removes the need for a schema
It moves the schema into the code that reads the documents, unless a validator holds the shared fields to rules
It rewrites old documents by itself when the shape changes
It can't store documents with different fields in one collection
quiz.why: A document store is schema-on-read by default: every program that reads must handle every shape ever written. A validator (in MongoDB 9.0, even at the `constraint` level) brings schema-on-write back for the fields you name. Nothing rewrites old documents for you (lesson 1).

quiz.q: A DynamoDB table has partition key `accountId` and sort key `createdAt`. Which request is one Query that reads only what it returns?
options: `merchantId = M-0042`, newest first
`accountId = A-1001 AND amountMinor > 5000`
`accountId = A-1001 AND createdAt BETWEEN 08:00 AND 12:00`
`createdAt > 09:00` for every account
quiz.why: It gives the partition key with `=` and one range on the sort key: one unbroken slice of one partition. A filter on `amountMinor` still reads the whole partition first, and the other two don't name a partition at all (lessons 2 and 3).

quiz.q: One DynamoDB item holds a shop's running total (one partition key, one sort key, under 1 KB). It's updated 1,200 times a second. What happens?
options: Writes beyond about 1,000 a second are slowed down or refused (throttled), whatever the table's capacity
Nothing, as long as the table's paid-for capacity is above 1,200 write units
DynamoDB splits the item over two partitions to take the load
The writes slow down only once the item passes 400 KB
quiz.why: One item lives in one partition, and each partition tops out at 1,000 write units and 3,000 read units a second, so capacity for the whole table can't help. DynamoDB can move a busy item into a partition of its own, but it can't split one item. Spread the writes over several keys (the same key with a number from 1 to 10 on the end, say) and add them up when you read. 400 KB is the largest item allowed (lesson 3).

quiz.q: A transfer takes money from A-1001 and adds it to A-2002 in DynamoDB. Which design keeps the two writes all or nothing?
options: Two UpdateItem calls with the same idempotency key
One BatchWriteItem with both updates
One TransactWriteItems, with the condition `balanceMinor >= :amt` on the side that takes money out, plus the side that adds it
A GetItem of the balance, a check in Kotlin, then two PutItems
quiz.why: TransactWriteItems applies every action or none, and checks the condition inside it. A batch can partly succeed and can't update with a condition. An idempotency key stops repeats, not half-done pairs. And a read outside the write can race with another writer (lesson 4).

quiz.q: Why is Cassandra called a wide-column store?
options: It stores each column's values together on disk, like a column store built for analysis
It has no columns, only opaque values
It allows any number of columns in an index
A partition is like a wide row: a partition key and a sorted list of rows, each with its own columns
quiz.why: The name comes from Bigtable's sparse rows, rows where most columns are empty. It isn't a column store, which keeps each column together so whole columns read fast. Stonebraker and Pavlo describe it as a document model with one level of nesting (lessons 1 and 5).

quiz.q: A Cassandra table is keyed `((merchant_id, day), created_at)`. The busiest shop takes 432,000 payments a day. What's the fix the guidance points to?
options: An hour bucket in the partition key, so a partition holds about 18,000 rows
A secondary index on `created_at`
Nothing: Cassandra splits large partitions across machines
Deleting old rows every night
quiz.why: A partition never splits, and the guidance is under 100,000 rows and 100 MB. Rows = write rate x bucket length, so a smaller bucket brings that table under. Deletes would add tombstones, not remove rows (lesson 5).

quiz.q: Refunds must never add up to more than the payment. In which designs can one write, with no transaction, check the rule and add a refund?
options: Only in a table with a CHECK constraint across rows
A MongoDB document with its refunds inside, or a PostgreSQL row whose jsonb holds them, each changed by one write with the check in it
Only with a Cassandra logged batch
None: the rule always spans several records
quiz.why: Put the refunds inside the record and the rule is about one record, which both stores change in one step, with the check in the filter or the WHERE. A CHECK constraint can't see other rows, and a logged batch is applied in full in the end but can be seen half done (lesson 6).

quiz.q: A recursive CTE over transfers between accounts uses `UNION ALL` and carries a `hops` column. The data has a cycle. What happens in PostgreSQL 18?
options: PostgreSQL notices the cycle and stops
It stops after 100 rounds
It runs until something cancels it; add a CYCLE clause or a path check
It raises an error before running
quiz.why: The loop stops only when a round produces no rows, and a cycle always produces more. PostgreSQL has no depth limit and notices no cycles. `CYCLE ... SET is_cycle USING path` or a path check stops it, and SQL/PGQ's `ANY SHORTEST` does the bookkeeping for you where it's available (lesson 7).

quiz.q: Which statement about graph query languages in November 2026 is accurate?
options: GraphQL is the ISO standard language for graph databases
PostgreSQL 19 ships SQL/PGQ's GRAPH_TABLE
Cypher was withdrawn when GQL was published
GQL (ISO/IEC 39075:2024) made Cypher-style patterns a standard, and SQL/PGQ puts the same patterns inside SQL in Oracle, Spanner Graph and DuckDB
quiz.why: GQL and SQL/PGQ share one pattern language, and Neo4j's Cypher 25 covers most of GQL's required features. PostgreSQL took SQL/PGQ out of 19's betas, and GraphQL is a query language for APIs, not a database language (lessons 7, 8 and 9).

quiz.q: A GraphQL query asks for 30 payments, each with its account and the account's customer. Resolvers fetch one record per call. After you add a batching loader for each type, how many backend calls does the query make?
quiz.why: One call per level: the payments, then all their different account ids in one call, then all the different customer ids in one call. Without batching it's 1 + 30 + 30 = 61, and the number grows with the page size (lesson 9).
